title: Test day two
hook: notice what's easy: Naaman storms off when the prophet tells him only to wash in the Jordan
tomorrow: a Guru's sons refused a muddy job. who carried it?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: test week. Daniel asked for ten days and an honest look. Today is day two of yours, and the first thing to notice is what's easy.

Some advice is so simple it almost sounds insulting: drink water, go to bed, call your mother. Naaman, commander of the army of Syria, got advice like that. He's a great man with leprosy. A captive girl from Israel, a servant in his house, says a prophet there could heal him. So he travels to Israel with horses, chariots and gifts, all the way to the prophet Elisha's door. Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger: go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and you'll be clean. And Naaman storms off in a rage.
screen: `DRINK WATER. GO TO BED.` → `A GENERAL AT THE PROPHET'S DOOR.` → `GO WASH IN THE JORDAN.` → `NAAMAN STORMS OFF.`

segments.voice: He says it out loud: I thought he would surely come out to me, call on the name of the LORD his God, and strike his hand over the place. Aren't the rivers of Damascus better than all the waters of Israel? Then his servants step in, with the line the story turns on: "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" So he goes down to the river and dips seven times, and his skin comes back like a little child's. Then he tries to pay, and Elisha refuses every gift. Here's the teaching. In this story from the Hebrew Bible, God's healing comes through a small, humble act, and it can't be bought. Notice who keeps rescuing Naaman: a captive girl, then his own servants. The small voices point him to the small cure. Naaman, the outsider, says before he leaves that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel. Jesus later names him in Luke's Gospel, a foreigner who was healed, and Christian readers hear grace in it: the gift is free, and the way in is plain. So on day two of a test week, the easy lines aren't cheating. They might be the river.
screen: `I THOUGHT HE WOULD COME OUT.` · `IF HE HAD BID SOME GREAT THING.` · `SEVEN DIPS, SKIN LIKE A CHILD'S.` · `THE GIFT IS FREE, THE WAY IS PLAIN.` · then, large: `EASY.`

segments.voice: Read your rule and say the easy lines out loud, one at a time, plainly, the way Elisha's message was plain: wash, and be clean. No apology for any of them. Then rest your hands, and let the easy things be enough for the rest of the time.
Test day two: notice what's easy, and don't despise it. Naaman's cure was a plain river, and it was free.
Take this with you: easy. If he'd asked some great thing, you'd have done it; so wash. Day 1692, down to the river.

screen: `DAY 1692 COUNTS.` → `YOUR RULE · 4 OF 12.` → `TOMORROW: A GURU'S SONS REFUSED A MUDDY JOB. WHO CARRIED IT?`

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the story of Naaman (2 Kings 5) as healing that comes through a humble act and can't be bought; Jesus recalls Naaman in Luke 4:27. In a test week of a rule of life, the easy lines are noted as honestly as the hard ones.

fork.setup: your coworker's doctor tells him to drink more water and sleep earlier. he wants "a real treatment." what fits Naaman's story?
options: the plain thing may be the cure; Naaman almost missed his for being too simple.
he's right: real help always comes from something big and dramatic.
simple advice means the doctor didn't take him seriously at all.
fork.reveal: Naaman expected a grand healing and nearly went home sick. His servants asked: if he'd bid some great thing, wouldn't you have done it? So wash.

trapdoor: what you thought: easy means not worth much.
what it means: in the story the cure is small, humble and free: wash, and be clean; and Elisha takes no payment.
what a scholar hears: 2 Kings 5:1-19 (the servant girl, the rivers of Damascus, the servants' plea, Elisha's refusal) and Luke 4:27, where Jesus names Naaman.

chat.says: day 2: the tea-and-one-breath line is so easy it feels like cheating. cut it?
options: keep it: Naaman almost skipped his cure because it was too simple. easy can be the river.
cut it; a practice only counts if it's hard enough to feel like a sacrifice.
keep it but add more steps, so it finally feels serious enough to count.
chat.meaning: Naaman wanted a great deed and nearly missed his healing. His servants asked why not just wash. In the story, the plain thing is the gift.

tie.story: Naaman stormed off when told simply to wash in the Jordan, until his servants talked him into it.
